name: THE PECORINO ON SOMEONE YOUR OWN SIZE BURGER (comes with pecorino crisps)

recipe.history:
Pecorino Romano is one of the oldest and most storied cheeses in the world, with roots stretching back over two thousand years to the pastoral hills surrounding ancient Rome. The name itself tells the story: pecora means sheep in Italian, and this sharp, hard cheese has been produced from the milk of Sardinian sheep — specifically the Sarda breed — for millennia. Roman legions carried it on long marches because of its durability and dense caloric content, and the cheese was so integral to Roman life that it was used as currency and rationed to soldiers alongside bread and olive oil. Its production spread from the Roman Campagna and the island of Sardinia throughout central Italy, particularly in Lazio, Tuscany, and Sardinia, where strict DOP (Denominazione di Origine Protetta) regulations now govern its production. The flavor is bold, salty, and assertive — nothing at all like the gentler Parmigiano-Reggiano it is often compared to — with a dry, crumbly texture that intensifies as the wheel ages past eight months.

Pecorino Romano made its way to American tables through the great waves of Italian immigration in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when millions of southern Italians and Sardinians arrived in cities like New York, Philadelphia, and Boston. These immigrants brought their foodways with them — their dried pasta, their cured meats, their beloved hard cheeses — and Pecorino Romano became a staple in Italian-American cooking long before Parmigiano-Reggiano was widely available or affordable in the United States. It found its footing in the burger world through the American love affair with cheese crisps and frico, the Italian technique of melting hard aged cheese directly onto a hot pan until it forms a lacy, crackling wafer. As gourmet burger culture exploded in the 2000s and chefs began reaching beyond the standard American and cheddar slices, Pecorino's sharp salinity became a natural foil for rich, fatty beef — both melted into the patty and crisped into shards that shatter pleasingly against the bite.

I remember the first time I truly understood Pecorino Romano as something more than just the cheese my aunt shook from a green cardboard canister over her Sunday gravy. I was maybe twelve, and she handed me a wedge broken directly from the wheel she kept wrapped in the back of her refrigerator. It was dry and crystalline and almost unbearably salty, and I didn't know what to do with it at first. Then she put a thin slice on a hot dry skillet — no butter, no oil, nothing — and I watched it bubble and blister and go golden and then I heard the crack when she lifted it off with a spatula. I ate that crisp standing at her stove and it tasted like the best chip I had ever had in my life. Every time I make pecorino crisps now, I am twelve years old again, standing in that small kitchen in the smell of Sunday tomato sauce, learning that the simplest alchemy is also the most profound.

Cooking a burger to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius — is not a preference or a suggestion. It is the only correct answer to the question of how a burger should be cooked, full stop. At medium rare, the fat within the grind has begun to render but has not fled the patty entirely; the proteins have set enough to hold their shape but retain that yielding, almost custardy give when you press gently on the surface. The juices run pink and freely when you cut through, pooling on the plate like something precious that should not be wasted. When you press a burger past this point — into the gray, steaming, squeezed-dry territory of medium well or well done — you are not cooking anymore, you are punishing. You are destroying the careful work of the butcher who selected and ground that beef, the farmer who raised the animal, and yourself, who had the opportunity to eat something magnificent and chose instead to eat a puck of dried protein. Medium rare is respect. Medium rare is understanding. Medium rare is the only way.
ingredients: 4 large eggs (3 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
6 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened and cubed
6 oz Pecorino Romano, finely grated (about 1 1/2 cups packed)
3 oz Pecorino Romano, shaved with a vegetable peeler
2 cloves garlic, minced to a paste
2 tablespoons fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
Kosher salt and white pepper to taste
1/2 small red onion, very thinly sliced
Flaky sea salt (Maldon or fleur de sel) for finishing
Extra virgin olive oil for finishing
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — DAY BEFORE: Combine warm milk, yeast, and 1 teaspoon of the sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let sit 5 to 8 minutes until foamy.
2. Add flour, remaining sugar, salt, and 3 eggs to the yeast mixture. Mix on low with the dough hook until just combined, about 2 minutes.

3. Increase speed to medium and mix for 6 minutes until a shaggy dough forms. Add softened butter one cube at a time, waiting for each piece to be incorporated before adding the next. This will take 8 to 10 minutes. The dough will be very soft and slightly sticky.
4. Increase speed to medium-high and mix another 6 to 8 minutes until the dough is smooth, elastic, and pulls cleanly from the sides of the bowl.
5. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and refrigerate overnight (8 to 12 hours).
6. The next day, remove dough from refrigerator. Divide into 6 equal portions (about 110g each). Shape each into a tight round ball by pulling the edges under and pinching at the bottom.
7. Place buns on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing 3 inches apart. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and let proof at room temperature for 2 to 3 hours until noticeably puffed.
8. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Beat remaining egg with 1 tablespoon water for egg wash. Brush tops of buns gently with egg wash. Sprinkle with sesame seeds if using.
9. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing.
10. MAKE THE PECORINO CRISPS: Line a baking sheet with a silicone mat or parchment paper. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C).

11. Toss the finely grated Pecorino with black pepper and red pepper flakes. Arrange into 6 mounds of about 3 tablespoons each on the prepared baking sheet, spacing well apart. Spread each mound into a flat round roughly 4 inches in diameter.

12. Bake 7 to 9 minutes, watching closely, until the crisps are uniformly golden and bubbling. They will look lacey and may still seem soft — they firm up dramatically as they cool. Remove from oven and allow to cool on the pan for at least 10 minutes before handling. Set aside.

13. MAKE THE LEMON-HERB AIOLI: In a medium bowl, whisk egg yolks, mustard, and garlic paste until smooth and slightly thickened. While whisking constantly, add the neutral oil in a very slow, thin stream, drop by drop at first, then increasing to a thin drizzle as the emulsion forms and thickens.

14. Once all neutral oil is incorporated, whisk in the olive oil in a slow stream. Whisk in lemon juice and zest. Fold in parsley and chives. Season generously with kosher salt and white pepper. Cover and refrigerate until needed.

15. FORM THE PATTIES: Combine ground chuck and ground short rib in a large bowl. Using your hands, gently mix just until the two grinds are combined — do not overwork. Season with salt, pepper, and garlic powder and fold in gently.

16. Divide into 6 equal portions (about 6 oz each). Form into round patties about 4 1/2 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple in the center of each with your thumb to prevent doming during cooking. Refrigerate on a parchment-lined tray for at least 20 minutes.
17. COOK THE PATTIES: Heat a cast-iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil.

18. Season the cold patties once more with a pinch of salt and pepper on both sides just before they hit the pan. Cook patties in batches, without pressing, for 3 minutes on the first side until a deep brown crust forms.

19. Flip once. Cook an additional 2 to 2 1/2 minutes. Check internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer — target 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Remove patties from heat and rest on a wire rack for 3 minutes. The temperature will rise slightly as they rest.
20. TOAST THE BUNS: While patties rest, split brioche buns and place cut-side down on the hot skillet for 60 to 90 seconds until golden and crisp.
21. ASSEMBLE: Spread a generous tablespoon of lemon-herb aioli on both cut sides of the bun. Place a butter lettuce leaf on the bottom bun. Add the rested patty.
22. Lay the shaved Pecorino Romano over the hot patty and allow it to soften slightly from the residual heat — about 30 seconds.
23. Top with tomato slices and red onion. Drizzle lightly with extra virgin olive oil and finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt.
24. Lean a pecorino crisp against the top bun or place it carefully on top of the assembled burger. Place the top bun and serve immediately alongside extra crisps.
